title: Douglas, Wyoming: Jackalope Capital
summary: The Wyoming town that invented America's favorite imaginary animal - where two taxidermist brothers in 1932 put antlers on a jackrabbit and created a creature that now has its own statue, hunting licenses, and world capital.

content.intro: Douglas, Wyoming, population 6,000, is the Jackalope Capital of the World. The town is home to a giant jackalope statue in the town center, issues official jackalope hunting licenses, and celebrates a creature that doesn't exist but should. The jackalope - a jackrabbit with antelope horns - was invented here in 1932 when Douglas Herrick, a young taxidermist, tossed a rabbit carcass on the floor and it landed next to some deer antlers. The result looked too good not to mount. Herrick and his brother Ralph sold their first jackalope mount to a local hotel, and the legend spread from there. Postcards, tall tales, and tourist dollars followed. The jackalope has since escaped Douglas to become American folklore, appearing on postcards, in cartoons, and in bars across the West. But Douglas was first, and Douglas is proud. Every June, the town hosts Jackalope Days. The hunting licenses stipulate that hunters must have an IQ below 72 and can only hunt between midnight and 2 AM.

sections.title: The Invention
sections.body: Douglas and Ralph Herrick were teenagers in Douglas, Wyoming, when they invented the jackalope. Their father, a taxidermist, had taught them the trade. In 1932, Douglas came home from hunting and tossed a jackrabbit carcass on the floor of the shop. It landed near a rack of deer antlers. Douglas saw the potential immediately. The brothers mounted the rabbit with antlers attached and sold it to Roy Ball, owner of the LaBonte Hotel in Douglas. The mounted jackalope hung in the hotel for decades, delighting guests and inspiring imitators. The Herricks continued making jackalopes until Douglas's death in 2003. By then, the creature had become legend.

sections.title: The Legend
sections.body: The jackalope developed elaborate mythology. According to legend, jackalopes are incredibly fast - they can run up to 90 mph. They can mimic human voices, calling out to hunters to confuse them. They mate only during lightning storms. Their milk is a powerful aphrodisiac (and can only be collected while the animal sleeps). They're aggressive when cornered, attacking with their antlers. The best way to catch one is to leave out whiskey; jackalopes love whiskey and become slow when drunk. None of this is true, obviously, but the accumulation of detail gives the jackalope a mythology as elaborate as any genuine animal's.

sections.title: The Capital
sections.body: Douglas embraced its creation. In 1965, the Chamber of Commerce declared Douglas the 'Jackalope Capital of the World.' A giant jackalope statue was installed in downtown, eight feet tall and wearing a saddle so children can climb on. The town issues jackalope hunting licenses - official-looking documents that permit hunting between midnight and 2 AM on June 31 (which doesn't exist). Jackalope Days, held every June, features a parade, crafts, rodeo, and general celebration of a fictional animal. The Herrick family is local royalty. Douglas is not embarrassed to be famous for inventing a fake animal. It's proud.

sections.title: The Spread
sections.body: The jackalope escaped Douglas to colonize American culture. Mounted jackalopes appeared in bars and restaurants across the West. Postcards showed jackalopes being milked, ridden, or simply observed. Ronald Reagan reportedly had a jackalope mount in his collection. The Pixar film 'Boundin'' featured a jackalope. The creature appears in video games, cartoons, and children's books. Scientists note that the legend may have origins in rabbits infected with Shope papilloma virus, which causes horn-like growths. But Douglas's jackalope - antlers carefully attached by teenage taxidermists - is the version that captured America's imagination.

sections.title: Visiting Douglas
sections.body: Douglas is located on Interstate 25 in eastern Wyoming, about 50 miles east of Casper. The giant jackalope statue is in downtown, at Third and Center streets. Jackalope hunting licenses are available at the Douglas Area Chamber of Commerce. Jackalope Days occurs annually in June. The Converse County Museum has Herrick jackalope mounts and local history. The Wyoming State Fairgrounds hosts the Wyoming State Fair in August. Douglas is also home to the Fort Fetterman historic site. Casper has the nearest commercial airport (Casper-Natrona County International). The town is small, quiet, and genuine - the kind of place that would invent a jackalope and never apologize for it.

content.flightContext: Located at 42.76°N, 105.38°W in eastern Wyoming along the North Platte River. From altitude, Douglas is a small town grid alongside I-25, surrounded by Wyoming ranchland. The North Platte River winds past to the south. Casper is 50 miles west. The terrain is high plains - brown grassland, occasional buttes, the Laramie Range visible to the south. Casper-Natrona County International Airport is the nearest commercial service. The isolation is total - Douglas is hours from any major city, exactly the kind of place where tall tales thrive.

strongOpinions: Douglas is not embarrassed to be famous for inventing a fake animal
